title: Impact of Class Size Cap Policy on Reading Scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of the class size cap policy on reading scores. The DID method is appropriate here because we have a treatment group (schools subject to the policy) and a control group (schools not subject to the policy), and we can observe the outcomes before and after the policy implementation.

The key assumption in DID is that, in the absence of the treatment, the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend over time. This assumption is often referred to as the "parallel trends" assumption.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s45_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data frame
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("unit_id", "period"))

# Run the DID regression
did_model <- plm(y ~ treat_x_post, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for the treatment effect
summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Estimate"]

# Robustness check: Clustered standard errors
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect the coefficient on the `treat_x_post` variable to be positive, indicating that the class size cap policy leads to an increase in reading scores. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the data, but we expect it to be small to moderate in size, as class size is just one of many factors that can influence student performance. The parallel trends assumption is crucial for the validity of our results, and any violations of this assumption could lead to biased estimates.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Comparative analysis of reading scores before and after the policy in treated and untreated schools.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The class size cap policy resulted in a decrease in reading scores.
